title: GOD ALLOWED SATAN TO TORMENT PAUL… BUT THE REASON WILL CHANGE HOW YOU SEE YOUR OWN SUFFERING
paragraphs: GOD ALLOWED SATAN TO TORMENT PAUL… BUT THE REASON WILL CHANGE HOW YOU SEE YOUR OWN SUFFERING

He begged God three times to take it away. Heaven answered him—but not with the miracle he expected. What Jesus revealed about that “messenger of Satan” may completely change the way you understand unanswered prayers, spiritual attacks, weakness, and the grace that refuses to let you go.

There is something deeply unsettling about a man who could heal the sick, cast out demons, endure persecution, and preach the resurrected Christ with extraordinary boldness… yet could not get God to remove the one thing that was tormenting him.
Think about that.
The apostle Paul had witnessed the power of Jesus Christ in ways most believers can barely imagine.

He had encountered the risen Lord on the road to Damascus. He had seen lives transformed through the Gospel. He had been entrusted with extraordinary revelations. God had used him to establish churches, confront darkness, and proclaim salvation to the Gentiles.
And yet…
Something was hurting him.
Something was humiliating him.
Something was pressing against his life so relentlessly that he pleaded with the Lord for relief.
Not once.
Not twice.
Three times.
And God did not remove it.
Why would a loving Father allow something Paul called a “messenger of Satan” to continue troubling one of His most faithful servants?
Was God angry with Paul?
Had Paul secretly failed?
Was his faith insufficient?
Or was something happening in Paul's suffering that could not be understood simply by looking at the pain?
Because if you have ever cried yourself to sleep after praying for a miracle that never came…
If you have ever watched someone else receive the breakthrough you desperately needed…
If you have ever wondered why the God who loves you has not stopped the thing that keeps breaking your heart…
Then Paul's story is not merely ancient history.
It may be closer to your life than you realize.
And before we reach the end, there is one sentence from Jesus that we must understand correctly.
Because it does not mean what many suffering Christians have been led to believe.
Paul tells us in 2 Corinthians 12:7 that because of the extraordinary revelations he had received, something was given to him that he describes in Greek as:
σκόλοψ τῇ σαρκί — skolops tē sarki
Literally, a thorn in the flesh.
The Greek word skolops can describe a pointed object, such as a thorn or stake. It communicates something painful and piercing. But Paul does not tell us precisely what his thorn was.
That matters.
Some have suggested a physical illness, perhaps involving his eyesight. Others have proposed severe opposition, persecution, or another persistent affliction.
The passage itself does not settle the question.
We should not pretend to know what Scripture has not revealed.
But Paul does tell us something about the thorn's character.
He calls it:
ἄγγελος Σατανᾶ — angelos Satana
A messenger of Satan.

The Greek word angelos means messenger and can refer to a human or angelic messenger depending on the context. Here, Paul identifies the messenger with Satan, but the exact nature of the affliction remains uncertain.
And then Paul uses another disturbing expression.
ἵνα με κολαφίζῃ — hina me kolaphizē
So that it might strike or buffet him.
The verb kolaphizō conveys the idea of striking with the fist or mistreating someone with blows.
This was not a minor inconvenience Paul was casually complaining about.
He describes an affliction that repeatedly battered him.
And here is where the story becomes theologically astonishing.
Paul says the thorn was given to keep him from becoming conceited because of the extraordinary revelations he had received.
Do you see the tension?
It was a messenger of Satan.
Yet God was accomplishing a purpose through what Paul suffered.
Satan's purposes are evil. God's purposes are holy.
Those truths are not contradictions.
They are the very reason this passage deserves our careful attention.
Consider Joseph.
His brothers sold him into slavery. Their betrayal was wicked. Their actions caused terrible suffering.
Yet years later, Joseph could say:
“You meant evil against me; but God meant it for good.”
That is Genesis 50:20, expressed here in the wording of the World English Bible.
Notice what Joseph did not say.
He did not call evil good.
He did not excuse his brothers.
He did not pretend the betrayal was harmless.
He recognized that God had worked through the evil intentions of others to accomplish a saving purpose.
The same distinction matters when we read Paul's testimony.
God's ability to bring good out of suffering does not make the suffering itself good.
And God's sovereignty over evil does not make Him morally evil.
The clearest example is the cross.
Human beings betrayed, condemned, mocked, and crucified the sinless Son of God.
Those actions were sinful.
Yet Acts 2:23 and Acts 4:27–28 teach that Christ's death also took place within God's redemptive purpose.
The greatest evil human hands ever committed became the occasion for the greatest act of redemption history has ever witnessed.
Not because evil suddenly became righteous.
But because evil could not overthrow the purposes of God.
And that brings us back to Paul.
The man who had received extraordinary revelations was also a man who remained dependent upon extraordinary grace.
Paul himself explains the purpose: to keep him from becoming conceited.
The Greek word translated as becoming conceited is related to hyperairō, meaning to exalt or elevate oneself excessively.
It is the danger of becoming spiritually inflated.
And perhaps this is where the passage begins to confront us.
We often imagine that the closer someone walks with God, the less vulnerable that person should become.
We assume greater spiritual maturity must always produce greater comfort.
We quietly believe that enough prayer, enough fasting, enough Scripture, and enough obedience should eventually make suffering unnecessary.
But Paul destroys that assumption.
Here was an apostle entrusted with remarkable revelation.
And still he needed grace.
Still he experienced weakness.
Still he had to depend on Christ.
His calling did not make him self-sufficient.
His revelations did not make him invulnerable.
His spiritual authority did not place him beyond the need for humility.
And neither does ours.
But be careful here.
This does not mean every sickness is God's punishment for pride.
It does not mean every depression, disability, financial crisis, betrayal, or family tragedy has been specifically sent to humble you.
Scripture does not authorize us to make those accusations.
In John 9:1–3, Jesus challenged the assumption that a man's blindness must be traced to a particular sin committed by him or his parents.
In Luke 13:1–5, Jesus rejected the idea that those who suffered terrible deaths were necessarily worse sinners than others.
Paul explains the purpose of his own thorn.
He does not give us permission to diagnose the secret purpose behind every other person's suffering.
Sometimes the most faithful response to a hurting person is not an explanation.
It is compassion.
A listening ear.
A prayer.
A meal.
A hand that stays when everyone else has gone home.
And this is something the Church must remember.
People who are bleeding do not always need someone to explain the wound. Sometimes they need someone to help carry them toward Jesus.
Now imagine Paul praying.
We do not know the exact words he spoke.
We do not know whether tears accompanied his petitions.
We do not know how long each season of pleading lasted.
But we do know that he asked the Lord three times for the thorn to depart.
Three times.
This was not a man who believed suffering should simply be accepted without prayer.
Paul asked for deliverance.
And there is something profoundly comforting about that.
It is not sinful to ask God to take away your pain.
It is not spiritual immaturity to seek healing.
It is not a lack of surrender to ask the Father for relief.
Jesus Himself prayed in Gethsemane that, if possible, the cup might pass from Him, while submitting Himself completely to the Father's will (Matthew 26:39).
Prayerful surrender and an honest desire for relief can exist together.
So when you whisper, “Lord, please take this away,” you are not necessarily demonstrating weak faith.
You may be doing exactly what Paul did.
But then comes the answer.
And it is one of the most breathtaking statements in the New Testament.
Jesus tells Paul:
Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου, ἡ γὰρ δύναμις ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται.
Arkei soi hē charis mou, hē gar dynamis en astheneia teleitai.
“My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.”
— 2 Corinthians 12:9, World English Bible
Read that again.
Slowly.
Jesus did not say that Paul's suffering was imaginary.
He did not accuse Paul of lacking faith.
He did not tell him that true believers never struggle.
He said:
My grace is sufficient for you.
The Greek word arkei, from arkeō, communicates sufficiency—being enough or adequate for what is needed.
And charis, grace, speaks of favor and gift.
In this passage, Christ assures Paul that His grace is enough for him even while the affliction remains.
But do not misunderstand this promise.
Jesus is not telling every suffering believer that every painful circumstance will remain unchanged.
Nor is He promising that believers will never experience exhaustion, grief, or overwhelming difficulty.
The promise in Paul's testimony is that Christ's grace is sufficient, and that His power can be displayed through human weakness.
Then comes the second half.
ἡ γὰρ δύναμις ἐν ἀσθενείᾳ τελεῖται
“For my power is made perfect in weakness.”
The Greek word dynamis means power.
Astheneia means weakness or infirmity.
And teleitai, from teleō, carries the sense of being brought to completion or reaching its intended expression.
Christ is not saying weakness is morally superior to strength.
He is revealing that His power does not depend upon Paul's natural adequacy.
His power can be fully displayed through a servant who knows he cannot sustain himself.
That changes everything.
Because some of us have spent years believing we must become stronger before God can truly use us.
We hide the tears.
We disguise the anxiety.
We conceal the questions.
We smile in church while quietly falling apart.
We tell people, “I'm blessed,” because we are afraid they will misunderstand what happens if we admit we are struggling.
We have learned how to sound victorious while feeling defeated.
And perhaps the most exhausting part is not even the pain itself.
It is the pressure to pretend the pain is not there.
But Paul did not build his testimony around pretending.
He spoke openly about weakness.
He acknowledged his need.
He described his unanswered request.
And then he pointed to Christ.
There is a difference between glorifying God through weakness and glorifying weakness itself.
Christianity does not ask us to celebrate abuse, neglect, exploitation, or preventable suffering.
It does not require a person to remain in danger to prove faithfulness.
Seeking medical care, counseling, protection, justice, and practical help is not a betrayal of Christ.
Paul himself made use of lawful protections when facing unjust treatment (Acts 22:25–29).
The Gospel does not teach helpless resignation in the face of wrongdoing.
It teaches dependence upon Jesus Christ in every circumstance.
And sometimes that dependence includes asking others for help.
But there is an even deeper truth hidden in the way Paul responds.
After hearing Christ's answer, he writes:
— 2 Corinthians 12:9, World English Bible
He does not say he has fallen in love with pain.
He says he has discovered something greater than his own strength.
The power of Christ.
Paul's joy is not rooted in the existence of the thorn.
It is rooted in the sufficiency of the Savior.
And now we arrive at something many Christians desperately need to hear.
An unanswered request for deliverance is not proof that God has abandoned you.
Paul prayed.
The thorn remained.
And Christ answered.
Not with the removal Paul requested, but with a revelation of grace.
That does not mean every unanswered prayer is answered in exactly the same way.
It does mean that the absence of the outcome we wanted is not, by itself, evidence of the absence of God's love.
Consider the person who has prayed for a broken marriage.
The parent who has pleaded for a wandering child.
The believer who has asked for healing and still wakes up in pain.
The person who has fought temptation, repented sincerely, sought help, and still knows what it means to struggle.
The Christian who has buried someone they begged God to spare.
Please hear this.
Paul's story is not permission for anyone to promise you that your circumstances will improve tomorrow.
Nor is it permission to tell you that if your faith were stronger, your miracle would already have happened.
What it offers is something both humbling and deeply hopeful.
Your suffering does not automatically cancel your relationship with God.
Your weakness does not disqualify you from receiving His grace.
Your unanswered prayer does not erase the finished work of Jesus Christ.
And your life is not beyond the reach of redemption.
But there is another danger we must confront.
Sometimes we use the language of grace while refusing the call to repentance.
We want Jesus to comfort us without correcting us.
We want His presence without His authority.
We want His promises while protecting the very sins He commands us to abandon.
That is not the Gospel Paul preached.
The same apostle who rejoiced in Christ's sufficient grace also called believers to holiness, obedience, and a transformed life.
Grace is not permission to continue in sin.
Paul asks in Romans 6:1–2 whether believers should continue in sin so grace may abound.
His answer is emphatic.
May it never be.
The grace that sustains us in suffering is also the grace that teaches us to renounce ungodliness (Titus 2:11–12).
And this is where the Gospel becomes deeply personal.
Because perhaps your greatest need today is not only relief from something happening to you.
Perhaps there is also something within you that needs to be surrendered.
A bitterness you have protected.
A secret sin you have excused.
A relationship you know is pulling you away from Christ.
A habit that has slowly hardened your conscience.
A pride that refuses correction.
Or a quiet unbelief that has begun to convince you that Jesus is no longer enough.
The answer is not to punish yourself until you feel worthy.
The answer is to come to Christ.
Confess what is true.
Turn from what is sinful.
Trust the Savior who died for sinners and rose again.
Because repentance is not an attempt to purchase forgiveness through suffering.
It is a turning toward the One whose mercy is greater than our sin.
First John 1:9 assures believers that God is faithful and righteous to forgive confessed sins and cleanse us from unrighteousness.
And Romans 8:1 declares that there is no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
That is not cheap comfort.
That is blood-bought grace.
Jesus Christ did not come merely to make difficult lives feel a little easier.
He came to save sinners.
He lived in perfect obedience.
He died for our sins.
He rose bodily from the dead.
And everyone who truly trusts in Him is called into a new life under His lordship.
This is why our message will always return to one truth:
Think of Paul before his conversion.
He was not merely a confused religious man.
He persecuted the Church.
He approved of Stephen's death.
He threatened believers.
He attempted to destroy the very movement he would later proclaim.
If you had met Saul before the Damascus road, you might have considered him one of the last people God would choose to preach the Gospel.
And yet Jesus confronted him.
Not because Saul had earned mercy.
Not because his record was admirable.
Not because he deserved a second chance.
But because the risen Christ is mighty to save.
The persecutor became a preacher.
The enemy of the Church became a servant of the Church.
The man who once tried to silence the name of Jesus spent the rest of his life proclaiming that name.
And still…
The redeemed apostle had a thorn.
That detail matters more than we often realize.
Conversion did not make Paul incapable of suffering.
Grace did not erase every earthly affliction.
Redemption did not turn him into a man who never needed help.
But Jesus had changed who Paul belonged to.
His past no longer defined his standing before God.
His weakness no longer determined the limits of Christ's power.
And his suffering could not separate him from the love of God in Christ Jesus.
This is the scandal of grace.
Not that God pretends our sins were harmless.
Not that every consequence disappears.
Not that believers are promised comfortable lives.
But that Jesus Christ saves the undeserving, sustains the weak, and completes the work He has begun in those who belong to Him.
And perhaps that is the part of Paul's story you needed most.
You may have a thorn.
But you are not the thorn.
You may have a painful history.
But your history is not your Redeemer.
You may be struggling.
But your struggle is not greater than the Lord who calls you to Himself.
And if you belong to Jesus, your suffering does not have the final word over your eternal future.
Christ does.
One day, the resurrection hope promised in Scripture will be fully revealed.
Revelation 21:4 speaks of a future in which God wipes away every tear and death, mourning, crying, and pain are no more.
That is not a guarantee that every thorn will disappear in this present life.
It is a promise that suffering will not have an eternal throne in God's new creation.
And what a day that will be.
No more graves.
No more hospital rooms filled with fearful waiting.
No more secret tears.
No more bodies breaking under the weight of mortality.
No more sin.
No more death.
Not because we finally became strong enough to defeat these enemies ourselves.
But because Jesus Christ has conquered sin and death.
Until that day, we pray.
We persevere.
We repent when we fall.
We encourage one another.
We seek help when we need it.
We proclaim the Gospel.
And we keep returning to the Savior whose grace is sufficient.
Maybe tonight you are the one who needs prayer.
Maybe you have spent so long encouraging everyone else that nobody realizes how exhausted you have become.
Maybe you are the person everyone calls strong.
The one who knows the Bible verses.
The one who keeps showing up.
The one who smiles for photographs.
The one who whispers, “Lord, I don't know how much longer I can carry this,” when nobody else is listening.
You do not need to perform strength before Jesus.
You can tell Him the truth.
He already knows.
And if this article has brought something painful or hidden to the surface, do not rush past that moment.
Bring it into the light of Christ.
Someone reading may need to know that they are not the only Christian who has ever prayed through tears.
You do not need to reveal private details to be honest.
Sometimes a simple testimony can encourage a weary soul.
Send it to someone who is grieving.
Let it reach the person who has been afraid to admit they are spiritually exhausted.
Not because sharing a post earns God's favor.
But because truth is worth passing on.
There may come a night when you need to return to 2 Corinthians 12 and remember what Jesus actually said.

And if you have not yet followed Gospel Warrior, we invite you to walk with this community as we continue opening Scripture, confronting sin with truth, encouraging wounded believers, and pointing people toward the saving grace of Jesus Christ.
Invite your family, friends, struggling believers, those who have grown spiritually indifferent, and even those who are still questioning Christianity to follow along.
Because discipleship is not merely about having an emotional moment.
It is about learning to follow Jesus faithfully, day after day.
And for those who want to help this ministry continue and grow, there is another invitation.
Gospel Warrior exists to proclaim Christ, share biblical truth, encourage repentance, strengthen believers, and make discipleship resources more accessible.
These resources are intended to help believers study Scripture more deeply, understand the Gospel more clearly, and grow in their walk with Jesus.
Keeping resources available, developing new material, and expanding outreach requires time, effort, and practical support.
Scripture teaches that those who proclaim the Gospel may receive material support (1 Corinthians 9:14), and that believers may generously participate in supporting good works (2 Corinthians 9:6–8).
But Scripture also teaches that giving should not be compelled.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving is to be done willingly, not reluctantly or under pressure.
That distinction matters.
You can glorify God through generosity in many ways—supporting your local church, caring for those in need, serving others, and helping faithful Gospel ministries.
Your contribution helps sustain the work and creates opportunities for more people to encounter biblical teaching and free discipleship resources.
These products are simply an additional thank-you.
They are not the heart of the invitation.
The heart of the invitation is the mission.
More Scripture shared.
More people encouraged to open their Bibles.
More struggling believers reminded of Christ's sufficiency.
More opportunities to proclaim repentance, forgiveness, and new life through Jesus.
Pray for the ministry.
Invite someone to read the Scriptures with you.
Use the free resources available to deepen your own walk with Christ.
Every faithful act of service matters, even when it never receives public recognition.
And if you are financially unable to give, please do not carry guilt over that.
The Gospel is not for sale.
God's grace cannot be purchased.
Jesus Christ is the Savior.
Gospel Warrior is only a ministry seeking to point people toward Him.
And now, before you leave, I want to bring you back to Paul.
The thorn.
The three requests.
The answer that did not look like deliverance.
Imagine how different the story would have been if Paul had written only about his visions, his revelations, and his victories.
We might have admired him.
We might have been impressed.
But many of us would have struggled to see ourselves in his story.
Instead, Paul allowed us to see his weakness.
And through that weakness, he directed our eyes toward the sufficiency of Christ.
That is why his testimony still speaks.
Not because every suffering Christian will receive the same explanation Paul received.
Not because we can decode the hidden purpose of every tragedy.
But because the Jesus who sustained Paul is the same risen Lord proclaimed by the Gospel today.
And His grace is not reserved for people who have everything together.
It is for sinners who come to Him in faith.
It is for believers who know their need.
It is for the weary who keep looking to Christ.
It is for those who have fallen and must repent.
It is for those whose lives bear scars that nobody else can see.
So bring your thorn to Jesus.
Ask Him for deliverance.
Ask Him for wisdom.
Ask Him for strength.
Seek the help you need.
Trust His Word more than the accusations of your fears.
And remember that the cross, not your circumstances, is the decisive demonstration of God's love for His people.
If your pain has not disappeared, do not conclude that the Savior has disappeared with it.
Paul's thorn did not become his greatest message.
Christ's sufficient grace did.
And perhaps, in a way you cannot yet see, your life can also bear witness to the Lord who is faithful in weakness.
Not every scar will make sense on this side of eternity.
Not every question will receive the answer we long for.
But the resurrection assures us that the story of those who belong to Jesus does not end in the grave.
So tonight, even if your voice trembles, you can pray:

“Lord Jesus, I do not understand everything You have allowed. I have asked You to remove things that still hurt. Forgive me for the sins I have tried to hide, and teach me to trust You without pretending my pain is small. Give me wisdom to seek help, courage to obey Your Word, and strength to endure what I cannot change today. Guard me from bitterness and pride. Help me remember that Your grace is sufficient and Your power is not limited by my weakness. Above everything, draw me nearer to You. Amen.”
And if there is one thing I hope stays with you long after you close this article, it is this:
The thorn may still be there when you wake up tomorrow—but it will never be more powerful than the Christ who conquered the grave.
